candidates.title: Ted inverts the most famous line in American sports-movie history
candidates.detail: Ted tells the squad there is crying in football. The sentence is built on 'There's no crying in baseball!' — Tom Hanks as Jimmy Dugan in A League of Their Own (1992), ranked 54th on AFI's 2005 list of the 100 greatest movie quotations. The film is a fictionalised account of the real All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, a women's league founded during the Second World War, and it was directed by Penny Marshall, the first woman director to take a film past $100m at the box office. In the same speech Ted names Beaches (1988) — directed by Garry Marshall, Penny's older brother, who also appears in A League of Their Own as the candy magnate who founds the league. So the line Ted inverts and the film he names come from a brother and sister. VERIFY CAREFULLY: the A League of Their Own connection is the hunter's reading of the sentence structure; no recap located states it as the show's intention. The Marshall facts are all independently documented.
candidates.moment: In the changing room, Ted tells the players they do not have to hide, apologise for, or be ashamed of what they feel — there is, he says, crying in football.

candidates.title: The player Ted picks to prove his point
candidates.detail: Ted's example of a man crying at work is Lionel Messi. The choice is load-bearing: Messi's tears are among the most reproduced images in the sport. He wept after Argentina won the 2022 World Cup final, and he wept again after Argentina lost the 2026 final to Spain in extra time on 19 July 2026. candidates.title: Ted does nothing, on purpose
candidates.detail: Finding Alice sobbing, Ted neither fixes the problem nor produces one of his stories with a lesson folded inside. He sits down next to her and breathes. Reviewers singled it out as the strongest scene of the season; several noted that Ted is managing his own panic at the same moment, so the two of them are sitting through separate crises side by side without addressing either. The interest here is that the show's most talkative character is shown that the useful thing is presence, not language.
candidates.moment: Alice breaks down where the team can be seen training. Ted sits beside her in their shared office and they breathe, wordlessly, together.

candidates.title: Alice left her on for a hat-trick, and knows exactly what she cost her
candidates.detail: Alice Chilton was an Arsenal academy player whose own career was ended by repeated anterior cruciate ligament injuries; coaching was the way she stayed in the game. In this episode she declines to substitute Gemma, who has already scored twice, so she can chase a third — and Gemma's knee goes. The guilt is specific rather than general: she is the one person in the building who knows precisely what she has handed her.
candidates.moment: Richmond are comfortably ahead. Gemma wants to stay on; Alice lets her. Minutes later Gemma comes off on a stretcher.

candidates.title: The injury the women's game cannot get out from under
candidates.detail: The episode builds its crisis on the single most-discussed structural problem in women's football. Published work puts women's ACL injury rates somewhere between two and eight times men's depending on the study and league, with football-specific work at the higher end; one large cross-league database found roughly fourfold variation between women's leagues, and no significant gap at all in some. Follow-up outcomes are worse too: women are markedly less likely to return fully, and re-tear rates within five years are high. The causes are genuinely contested — anatomy, hormonal cycle, pitch and boot design, training load and the historic under-resourcing of women's medical provision are all argued. NOTE: the show does not name Gemma's injury as an ACL tear; it is a knee injury awaiting an MRI. Do not close that gap.
candidates.moment: A knee goes in a match Richmond are already winning, and the club discovers it has no functioning medical answer.

candidates.title: Roy's tribute is on a real wall, and a real woman got there first
candidates.detail: Roy is honoured at Chelsea's Shed Wall — an actual installation at Stamford Bridge, built from the surviving section of the old Shed End terrace, carrying portraits and biographies of club legends including Peter Osgood, Ray Wilkins, Peter Bonetti, Frank Lampard, Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink and John Terry, with QR codes for visitors. In 2024 Emma Hayes was added at the CFC Awards on her departure after twelve years and fifteen trophies as manager of Chelsea Women — the first of the women's legends to appear there. A fictional Chelsea legend collects his tribute in the episode where the show is arguing hardest for the women's team.

candidates.title: The title is a correction to a line that was never really said
candidates.detail: Higgins finds supporters quietly selling shares, some well above value, and cannot work out who is buying. Mae's advice — follow the anger — supplies the episode's title and reframes the search: stop asking who profits and start asking who is aggrieved. It sits directly against 'follow the money', which most people believe came out of Watergate. It did not: the line is Hal Holbrook's as Deep Throat in the 1976 film All the President's Men, screenplay by William Goldman. Mark Felt, later confirmed as Deep Throat, is not documented saying it, and it does not appear in Woodward and Bernstein's book. NOTE: the 'follow the money' contrast is the hunter's reading; no recap states it. The Goldman attribution is independently documented and is exactly the kind of misattribution this app already flags for Whitman.
candidates.moment: In the pub, Higgins lays out the share-buying he cannot explain, and Mae tells him to follow the anger instead.

candidates.title: The club doctor walks, and the plot follows
candidates.detail: Richmond's doctor, Strudwick, has been covering both the men's and the women's teams without a corresponding rise in pay, and cuts ties with the club. That is why Gemma lies at home undiagnosed while the squad waits on an MRI — the injury crisis is administrative before it is medical. It reads as the direct continuation of the previous episode's argument about what the women's team is paid, moved from the players to the staff: a club can announce a women's side and simply not fund the second set of everything it requires.

candidates.title: The BELIEVE sign gets edited by committee
candidates.detail: In the opening montage the players start sticking their own addenda onto the BELIEVE sign until it is buried in Post-its — one turning it into a threat, another softening it into a pleasantry. Recaps read it as the squad applying Alice's 'yes, and' lesson from the previous episode to the club's oldest object: accept what you are handed, then add something of your own. That is a real change in the sign's meaning. For three seasons it was Ted's, handed down; here it is amended by the people underneath it. NOTE: one recap reports Ted himself adding a line about letting it out; others describe only the players' Post-its. Do not state the wording of any individual note as settled.

candidates.title: The crying episode was written by the panic-attack writer
candidates.detail: 'Follow the Anger' was written by Jamie Lee and Brett Goldstein and directed by Erica Dunton. Jamie Lee also wrote 'Man City' (Season 2, Episode 8) — the episode in which Ted's panic attack sends him off the touchline and he tells Dr Sharon about his father's suicide, and in which Jamie Tartt punches his father in the changing room. The same writer who put Ted's worst hour on screen has now written the hour in which Ted sits with somebody else through theirs and tells a room full of players that crying is allowed at work. Goldstein, meanwhile, co-wrote the episode in which his own character is inducted onto a legends wall and uses the microphone to talk about somebody else.

candidates.title: Handed a microphone about himself, Roy talks about her
candidates.detail: Roy resists the induction from the start, and the journey there collapses into farce — a failed smart car, a claustrophobic stretch on the Underground, a scooter. When he finally gets to the microphone in front of an almost empty room, he does not talk about his career. He talks about Keeley and what she is worth, and about what she makes him feel he is worth. Reviewers read his whole resistance to the ceremony as an inability to accept praise rather than indifference to it.
candidates.moment: The ceremony has mostly dispersed. Roy speaks anyway, to a handful of people, and the speech turns out not to be about football.

candidates.title: The song on the Underground
candidates.detail: One review names the needle-drop over the Roy-and-Keeley Tube sequence as 'When I Get My Hands on You', crediting it with easing Roy's claustrophobia as it builds the scene. SHAKY — flagged for the reviewer. Only one source names the track, and the title is ambiguous: there is a 1973 country single of that name by Diana Trask, and a 2014 recording by The New Basement Tapes in which Marcus Mumford sets unused 1967 Bob Dylan lyrics to his own music, produced by T Bone Burnett. If it is the latter, the link is worth having — Mumford wrote and performs Ted Lasso's theme — but nothing located confirms which recording is used. Do not assert the Dylan/Mumford version without a second source.
